questions.problem: Given that ${y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)-2{x}^{2}=5,$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)-2{x}^{2} & =5 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)-2{x}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(y))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}) & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})-4x & =0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(3{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)) & =4x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4x}{3{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that  $y-{2}^{y}=3{x}^{2},$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}y-{2}^{y} & =3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y-{2}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({2}^{y}) & =6x \\ (1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2){2}^{y})(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =6x\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,{2}^{y}) & =6x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6x}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\,{2}^{y}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x)-{y}^{2}=y,$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x)-{y}^{2} & =y \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x)-{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(3x))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) \\ 3{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)-2y(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3{sec}^{2}⁡(3x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(2y+1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{sec}^{2}⁡(3x)}{2y+1}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that  ${e}^{y}=2y-x,$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2y-x) \\ {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}(2y)}{\text{d}x}-\frac{\text{d}(x)}{\text{d}x} \\ {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(2-{e}^{y}) & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2-{e}^{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for ${x}^{2}y+4y=2{x}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y+4y & =2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y+4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ [{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\cdot 2x]+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}-2xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+4) & =6{x}^{2}-2xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6{x}^{2}-2xy}{{x}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $2{x}^{3}y+2{y}^{2}=4{x}^{2}+6.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $2{x}^{3}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}y+2{y}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}+6 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}y+2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+6) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}y)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+6) \\ [2{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\cdot 6{x}^{2}]+4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8x \\ 2{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{x}^{2}y+4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8x-6{x}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}+4y) & =8x-6{x}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{8x-6{x}^{2}y}{2{x}^{3}+4y}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $7{x}^{3}{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2}=12{x}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $7{x}^{3}{y}^{3}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}7{x}^{3}{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2} & =12{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7{x}^{3}{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7{x}^{3}{y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{2}) \\ [21{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+21{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]+6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =24x \\ 21{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+21{x}^{2}{y}^{3}+6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =24x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}21{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =24x-21{x}^{2}{y}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(21{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+6y) & =24x-21{x}^{2}{y}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{8x-7{x}^{2}{y}^{3}}{7{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+2y}\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $2xy+4{y}^{3}={x}^{2}-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $2xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy+4{y}^{3} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2xy+4{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-1) \\ [2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y]+12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y+12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x-2y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(2x+12{y}^{2}) & =2x-2y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x-2y}{2x+12{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x-y}{x+6{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for ${x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+4{y}^{4}=6{x}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

 Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+4{y}^{4}=6{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+4{y}^{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(y))+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{y}^{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{3}) \\ [{x}^{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)]+16{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =18{x}^{2} \\ -{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+16{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =18{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+16{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =18{x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(16{y}^{3}-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)) & =18{x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{18{x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)}{16{y}^{3}-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point
questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,-1)$ for the curve ${x}^{2}y=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-1) \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y)+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\cdot 2x & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,-1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(1,\,-1)} \\  & ={(-\frac{2y}{x})}_{(1,\,-1)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot (-1)}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(4,\,4)$ for the curve $\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2}+{y}^{1/2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(4,\,4)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =-{\frac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}}}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{4}}{\sqrt{4}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{2} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},\,2)$ for the curve $y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =0 \\ y(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},\,2)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(\pi /3,\,2)} \\  & ={(\frac{y\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)})}_{(\pi /3,\,2)} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point
questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,1)$ for the curve ${x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2x+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y-2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ (2x+y)+(x-2y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x+y}{x-2y}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(0,\,1)} \\  & ={(-\frac{2x+y}{x-2y})}_{(0,\,1)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 0+1}{0-2\cdot 1} \\  & =-\frac{0+1}{0-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining an Intercept of a Tangent or Normal Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form
questions.problem: The equation of a curve is ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$ The normal line at the point $(-3,\,1)$ on the curve intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(-3,\,1).$  Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x-6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x}{-6y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(-3,\,1)$ is 

 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(-3,\,1)} \\  & ={(\frac{x}{3y})}_{(-3,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{3\cdot 1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is ${m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-1}=1.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(-3,\,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-1) & =1(x+3) \\ y & =(x+3)+1 \\ y & =x+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+4 \\ 0 & =x+4 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-4,\,0).$

The equation $xy=5$ represents a hyperbola. The tangent line at the point $(1,5)$ on the hyperbola intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,5).$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5) \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-y}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,5)$  is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(1,\,5)} \\  & ={(-\frac{y}{x})}_{(1,\,5)} \\  & =-\frac{5}{1} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(1,\,5)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-5) & =-5(x-1) \\ y & =-5(x-1)+5 \\ y & =-5x+10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-5x+10 \\ y & =-5\cdot 0+10 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,10).$

The coordinates of $P$ are $($

questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(2,1).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy & =6{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ 2x+(y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ 2x+y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ (x-12y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & ={(\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y})|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-2(2)-1}{2-12(1)} \\  & =\frac{(-5)}{(-10)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=-2.
$$

We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(2,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-2(x-2) \\ y-1 & =-2x+4 \\ y & =-2x+5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+5 \\ y & =-2(0)+5 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,5).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(1,\,2 \right)$ for the curve $xy+y^2=2x^2+4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y = y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+4) \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x \\ (x+2y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4x-y}{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(1,\,2 \right)$ is given by

$$
\eqalign{
m
&=\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right)_{\left(1,\,2 \right)}\[5pt]
&=\left(\dfrac{4x-y}{x+2y}\right)_{\left(1,\,2 \right)}\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{4\cdot 1-2}{1+2\cdot 2}\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{2}{5} \, .
}
$$

The equation $x^2-2x+y^2+4y=5$ represents a circle. The normal line at the point $\left(0, -5 \right)$ on the circle intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13947863/assets/b6c52a76654a4a545d356890d4deb04c74301e4091422a51e84551aeb3ec1152.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(0,-5).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, $m',$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m' = -\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y = y(x).$

$$
\eqalign{
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (x^2-2x+ y^2+4y)
	&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (x^2)-\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (2x)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (y^2)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (4y)&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\[5pt]	
	
	2x-2+2y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}+4\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=0\[5pt]	
	
	
	(2y+4)\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=2-2x\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
	&=\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}
	
}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ is 

$$
\eqalign{
	m
	&=\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\[5pt]
	&=\left(\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2-2\cdot 0}{2\cdot (-5)+4}\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2}{-6}\[5pt]
	&=-\dfrac{1}{3} \, .
	
}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=3.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
	y-y_1 &=m'\left(x-x_1 \right)\[5pt]
	y+5 &=3\left(x-0 \right)\[5pt]
	y&=3x-5
}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	y&=3x-5\[5pt]
	0&=3x-5\[5pt]
	x&=\dfrac{5}{3}
}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left(\dfrac{5}{3},\,0 \right).$
